title: Finding Unenumerated Rights: Two Methods
short: Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) asks for a "careful description" of the asserted right and whether it is deeply rooted in the Nation's history and tradition; another approach, from Justice Harlan's dissent in Poe v. Ullman (1961) and used in Obergefell (2015), treats tradition as a living one and reasons from principle.
trouble: Students treat one method as the law's clear answer. Present each in its best form: Glucksberg's supporters stress restraint and democratic choice; its critics say a narrow description of the right can decide the case in advance.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Some rights the Court protects are not named in the Constitution: to marry, to raise one's children, to refuse medical treatment. How does a judge decide which unnamed (unenumerated) liberties the Due Process Clause protects? Two methods, which you met in general form in originalism and living constitutionalism, divide the justices.

head: History and tradition (Glucksberg)
Reasoned judgment (Harlan in Poe; Obergefell)
rows: Justice Harlan's dissent in Poe v. Ullman (1961); used in Obergefell v. Hodges (2015)
a "careful description" of the asserted right, stated narrowly
identify the interest at stake in a broader principle (for example, marriage)
is it "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition" and "implicit in the concept of ordered liberty"?
does it fit the "rational continuum" of liberty, judged by a tradition that "is a living thing"?
history and tradition guide the inquiry but "do not set its outer boundaries" (Obergefell)
a right to marry for same-sex couples (Obergefell, 2015)

blocks.html: Supporters of the history and tradition method say it restrains judges. Rights not written in the text should be ones the nation has long recognized, so that judges do not substitute their own values for the people's; everything else is left to democratic choice. Its critics say a narrow description of a right can decide a case before it starts: almost no new claim was "deeply rooted" when described in very specific terms, and the method can freeze past injustices. Supporters of reasoned judgment say the Constitution protects principles of liberty that later generations may see more clearly, guided by precedent and history. Its critics say it gives judges too much room to declare rights that the people never adopted. The justices who use each method all claim to respect both history and the limits of the judicial role; they disagree about how.

doc.title: Justice Harlan, dissenting in Poe v. Ullman (1961)
doc.source: Poe v. Ullman, 367 U.S. 497, 542 (1961), Harlan, J., dissenting
paras: The balance of which I speak is the balance struck by this country, having regard to what history teaches are the traditions from which it developed as well as the traditions from which it broke. That tradition is a living thing.

marks.text: That tradition is a living thing
marks.note: Harlan's view: tradition grows; judges reason from it, not just list old practices.

blocks.cap: Harlan's words, often quoted in later cases.

blocks.html: Two methods for unenumerated rights: Glucksberg asks for a careful description of the right and whether it is deeply rooted in history and tradition; Harlan's Poe dissent, followed in Obergefell, reasons from broader principles with tradition as a living guide. Each has serious defenders; describe each fairly.

blocks.title: Describing the right
blocks.q: A patient claims a right to choose an experimental drug not yet approved. Under Glucksberg, what is the first step?
steps: Give a careful, specific description: "a right of a terminally ill patient to obtain a drug not yet approved," not "a right to make medical decisions."
Then ask whether that specific right is deeply rooted in the nation's history and tradition.
If not, rational basis review applies to the law.
blocks.a: Describe the right narrowly and carefully, then look to history and tradition.

blocks.title: Which method?
blocks.q: A majority opinion says that history and tradition "guide and discipline" the inquiry "but do not set its outer boundaries." Which approach is this, and which case?
steps: The sentence treats history as a guide, not a limit.
That is Obergefell v. Hodges (2015), following the reasoned-judgment approach.

blocks.html: Treating one method as the law's clear answer. The Court has used both, and the justices disagree. Present each in its best form: Glucksberg's supporters stress restraint and democratic choice; its critics say a narrow description of the right can decide the case in advance. Reasoned judgment's supporters stress principle and growth; its critics stress unchecked judicial power.
